newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar's Ratsiraka holds on to slim poll lead.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar's Ratsiraka holds on to slim poll lead.

text.p: Madagascar's former military ruler Didier Ratsiraka held on to a slim lead on Thursday in the race for the presidency of the Indian Ocean island with two-thirds of the votes counted.

Ratsiraka, a 60-year-old ex-Marxist and retired admiral, led with 51.4 percent of the vote against 48.6 percent for former president Albert Zafy, 69, according to results issued by the Interior Ministry.
It said 51 percent of Madagascar's 6.5 million registered voters turned out for Sunday's second-round runoff compared with a turnout of 60 percent in a first round on November 3.
Zafy supporters accused ministry officials on Thursday of manipulating computer results in favour of Ratsiraka. The ministry temporarily suspended issuing results to check on the charges.
A final result will probably not be known until next week because of poor communications on the island.
But Ratsiraka supporters proclaimed victory based on already published results, arguing that some 84,000 votes separated the two candidates and it was too late for Zafy to catch up.
Election observers from the Organisation of African Unity, the International Committee of Jurists and the Francophone Agency for Technical and Cultural Cooperation said the election was normal.
The vote was called after Zafy, who won 1993 elections over Ratsiraka, was impeached by parliament last July for abuse of his authority and for exceeding his constitutional powers.
Ratsiraka returned home from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September to stand against Zafy.
Political analysts, who before the election forecast an easy Ratsiraka victory, said results from rural polling stations were strengthening Zafy's position as his power base was in the interior.
Zafy was expected to beat Ratsiraka in two out of Madagascar's six provinces -- Antsiranana in the north and Toliara in the south. But both are less populous than the rest of the island.
None of the 15 candidates in the first round in November won 50 per cent of votes to secure outright victory. Ratsiraka led the first-round poll with 36.6 percent against 23.4 percent for Zafy.
Ratsiraka said on state radio on Sunday he was confident of winning but would support Zafy if he scored an upset victory.
Ratsiraka ruled for 16 years and has campaigned on promises of establishing a "humanistic and ecological republic" in Madagascar, where 14 million people live in chronic poverty.
Political squabbling under Zafy since 1993 in the former French colony has frustrated plans to improve life for the islanders, who remain among the poorest people in the world.
